title: Judgment: heuristics and biases
note: We rarely have the time or information to weigh every option, so we lean on heuristics, fast mental shortcuts that usually work. They also produce biases: systematic, predictable errors. Knowing the common ones (availability, representativeness, anchoring, framing, confirmation) lets you catch them and slow down when a decision matters.

read.title: Six hundred lives, two frames
text: Imagine an outbreak expected to kill 600 people. Program A will save 200 people for sure. Program B has a one-third chance of saving all 600 and a two-thirds chance of saving no one. Most people choose A, the sure thing.

Now the same choice is described differently. Under Program C, 400 people will die for sure. Under Program D, there is a one-third chance that nobody dies and a two-thirds chance that all 600 die. This time most people choose D, the gamble.

Look closely and A is identical to C, and B is identical to D. Only the wording changed. When outcomes are framed as gains, people tend to be risk averse; when the same outcomes are framed as losses, they tend to take risks. Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory explains this: we judge outcomes as gains or losses from a reference point, and losses loom larger than equal gains.

Framing is one of many predictable biases. Herbert Simon argued that our rationality is bounded by limited time, information and attention, so we rely on shortcuts. The fix is not to give up shortcuts but to notice when a decision is important, restate the problem in a second way, and see whether your answer survives the change.
